did_you_know.text: The king of Hazor called for allies — in Canaanite city-states kings sometimes formed coalitions when facing a common threat.
The phrase "people like the sand" and "many horses and chariots" underlines that chariots were a key symbol of military power in that era.
The "waters of Merom" are often identified with the Hula Basin in the north, a strategic area controlling water routes and fertile land.
The order to remove horses and burn chariots aimed to neutralize the enemy's military strength and prevent future use of those assets.
The text calls Hazor "head of all the kingdoms" — Hazor was a major city in northern Canaan and has archaeological destruction layers.
The phrase "no soul was left" reflects the religious concept of herem; scholars often view it as ritual language or literary exaggeration rather than a literal archaeological report.
The reference to towns on 'tels' recalls what a tel is — a mound of successive settlement layers where people rebuilt, so not every tel was completely burned down.
The Anakim are portrayed in the Bible as very tall people; here it says some remained in Philistine cities such as Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.
